Incircle And Midpoints

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and watch a line that always cuts two sides exactly in half.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a finger or mouse, or focus one and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the circle and the guiding lines.
Look for the math

Draw a triangle, put a circle inside it touching all three sides, and join two of the touch points. The purple line in the picture always hits the other two sides at their middles. The circle and the extra lines are just clues: the fact stays true however you move the corners.

Equal steps from the corners

The circle inside the triangle is its incircle. Two tangents drawn from the same corner to a circle have the same length, so AM = AK, BM = BN and CK = CN. Turn on hint 1 to see the matching tick marks on those pairs of side pieces.

A halfway point hidden in a bigger triangle

Draw through A a line parallel to the side BC. It meets MN at U and KN at V. The little triangle BMN is isosceles, and the similar triangle AMU must be isosceles too: AM = AU. The same reasoning gives AK = AV. Since AM = AK, we get AU = AV: A is the midpoint of UV. Hint 2 shows U, V and the equal angles.

Three parallels finish the job

Now look at triangle NUV. A is the midpoint of one side, and the lines AD and AE were drawn parallel to the other two sides. So D is the midpoint of NU and E is the midpoint of NV. That makes DE parallel to UV and to BC, and a line parallel to the base cuts any line across the triangle in half. In particular it cuts AB at F and AC at G, both midpoints. The three touch points K, M, N form the triangle Bogomolny calls the Gergonne triangle.

The logic test confirms every step on thousands of triangles: the largest departure from AF = FB and AG = GC is far below a millionth of a drawing unit, and each constructed point matches a second transcription of the applet's own method.

Turn on both hints and drag a corner until the triangle is very thin. Which equal-length pairs stay easy to see, and which ones crowd together?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
